title: Integration discovery - Nebula Healthcare
header: 2026-06-17 15:00 PST | Duration: 45m | Redwood: Maya Chen, Derek Patel, Alex Ruiz | Nebula Healthcare: Priya Rao, Liam O'Connor, Sara Gomez, Mark Tan
summary: Exploratory integration discussion focused on how Nebula Healthcare would connect to Redwood (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Key topics: SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, gateway/proxy architecture, rate limits and quota models, observability hooks (tracing, token-level cost breakdown), and security controls (SSO, KMS, audit logs). Customer leaning toward Dedicated or Private due to PHI concerns; wants a POC to validate latency and end-to-end observability before procurement.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, with Derek and Alex from our SE team. How are you all?
[00:08] Priya Rao: Good, thanks. Quick intro - I'm Priya, CTO at Nebula Healthcare. We've got Liam, Sara, and Mark here.
[00:15] Liam O'Connor: Hi all. We're excited to see integration options. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for PHI workloads.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Great. High level, we'll cover integration patterns — SDKs, LangChain and LlamaIndex support, and networking models incl VPC/private deploy. Then we can talk quotas and observability. Derek, want to kick off on SDKs?
[00:31] Derek Patel: Sure. We have REST and official SDKs for JS, Python, and Go. The Python SDK has first-class support for streaming and chunked responses; there's also a LangChain adapter and a LlamaIndex connector we ship as examples.
[00:44] Mark Tan: Quick question, the LangChain adapter — is it maintained upstream or are we expected to wrap?
[00:49] Alex Ruiz: We maintain our own adapter repo and upstream community contributions are welcome. For most customers we provide example notebooks showing Lang Chain (sometimes spelled LangChain), Llama Index integration and best practices like async batching and KV-cache warmups.
[01:05] Priya Rao: When you say KV-cache warmups, do you mean you persist model KV cache between requests? How does that work with multiple workers?
[01:14] Derek Patel: Good callout. We provide automatic prefix and KV caching at the routing layer for dedicated/private deployments. We shard cache per model variant and session id; for hosted there's a managed cache with TTLs. For private, you can configure cache persistence policies — there's some nuance with multi-worker consistency but our runtime handles eviction and staleness bounds.
[01:33] Liam O'Connor: Sounds promising. For latency-sensitive flows we need sub-150ms single token latency for short prompts. Do you have benchmark numbers for that on your dedicated pools?
[01:43] Maya Chen: We publish performance profiles in the model catalog, but actual latency depends on model, sequence length, and batching. Derek, can you share example numbers?
[01:52] Derek Patel: On our dedicated A100-style pools, for a 2k-context LLM proxy with quantization, we see ~120-180ms first-token latencies for smaller models and better batch sizing. We also offer configs to prioritize latency (lower batching) at throughput cost.
[02:09] Sara Gomez: Security question — we handle PHI, so encryption-at-rest, KMS integration, and audit logs are must-haves. How do private and dedicated differ here?
[02:18] Alex Ruiz: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in our infra but logs and control plane remain in Redwood unless you opt for Private. Private (VPC or on-prem) puts the control plane in your network and supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit log sinks to your SIEM. We are SOC2 compliant and can share attestation docs.
[02:36] Sara Gomez: Do you offer SSO/SAML and fine-grained RBAC? We need role separation for ops vs devs.
[02:41] Maya Chen: Yes. SSO via SAML and SCIM provisioning, and RBAC with custom roles available on enterprise plans. For Private, you can tie into your IdP directly.
[02:50] Mark Tan: Back to the SDK — rate limiting, how are limits enforced? We have bursty traffic from nightly jobs and also real-time user queries.
[02:58] Derek Patel: Rate limits are enforced at the API gateway. For hosted we have tenant-level quotas + per-key rate limits. Dedicated customers can configure higher baseline and burst windows; Private you control via your gateway. We also expose headers to show remaining quota and rate-limit reset.
[03:12] Liam O'Connor: Is there a recommended gateway/proxy pattern? We operate behind our own proxy and would prefer to keep a single egress point.
[03:19] Alex Ruiz: We see two patterns: 1) direct integration where your services call Redwood SDK/gateway; 2) edge-proxy pattern where you route traffic through your gateway (for logging, IP allowlists). For hosted, you can use a reverse proxy but you'll need to pass through authentication tokens; for Private, you can run our gateway-sidecar inside your network for mutual TLS and zero-trust.
[03:38] Priya Rao: Observability — we need token-level cost breakdowns and per-request traces that link back to our request ids. Does Redwood provide hooks?
[03:46] Derek Patel: Yes — we provide tracing headers you can pass (x-request-id -> appears in Redwood traces), and our Console surfaces per-route token counts and cost breakdown. We also have webhooks and a metrics Prometheus endpoint for latency and error rates. For PII/PHI we can filter or redact payloads before logs are persisted on hosted.
[04:06] Sara Gomez: What's the default data retention for logs? And can we ship logs to our SIEM?
[04:11] Alex Ruiz: Default retention is 30 days on hosted; enterprise add-ons allow longer retention and direct log exports to S3 or your SIEM. Private gives you full control.
[04:20] Mark Tan: For embeddings, is there a matching store you recommend? We currently use an internal vector DB but need compatibility with LlamaIndex.
[04:27] Derek Patel: LlamaIndex connectors include examples for Pinecone, Milvus, and Postgres-based vector stores. If you're using an internal store, we suggest running a thin adaptor layer — the SDK samples include that pattern.
[04:37] Liam O'Connor: On pricing, curious about token-based billing plus reserved capacity pricing for Dedicated. Can you outline the tradeoffs?
[04:44] Maya Chen: Sure. Hosted is pay-as-you-go per token/embedding plus request fees; Dedicated includes committed baseline for GPU capacity (monthly) with lower per-token compute costs and predictable latency; Private is custom pricing—platform license plus infra. Derek will send a pricing matrix.
[04:58] Priya Rao: We need to validate quality/regressions. Do you have built-in evals or integration with our internal eval suite?
[05:04] Derek Patel: We have Redwood Optimize features—automated evals, regression alerts against prompt sets, and you can upload your eval datasets. For POC, we can run canary rollouts and guardrails with automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if quality drops.
[05:18] Mark Tan: About SDK errors — is streaming resumable if the connection drops? We get flaky mobile connections.
[05:25] Alex Ruiz: Streaming is chunked and resumable to a point — we provide session ids and chunk offsets in the stream metadata. For critical flows we recommend idempotency keys and a small buffering layer on the client.
[05:37] Liam O'Connor: For the POC we want to benchmark: latency, throughput, token-cost, and end-to-end observability. Can Redwood run a load test in our staging with synthetic traffic?
[05:45] Maya Chen: Yes — we do joint benchmarks. For Dedicated/Private we can provision a temporary pool and run benchmark scripts; we'll need an NDA for deeper infra telemetry.
[05:56] Priya Rao: Timeline — procurement wants a 6-8 week window to decide. We aim to finish POC in 3 weeks. Is that feasible?
[06:03] Derek Patel: Tight but doable. We'll propose a POC plan: week 0 kick-off, week 1 integration + basic tests, week 2 load tests and observability checks, week 3 review and decision.
[06:13] Sara Gomez: One more security ask — can you provide an architecture diagram for Private deploy and a list of control plane endpoints we need to allow?
[06:20] Alex Ruiz: Yes, we'll include that in the security package. We'll also include SOC2, pen-test summaries, and KMS integration docs.
[06:29] Mark Tan: Are there any gotchas with LlamaIndex — memory usage or tokenization differences?
[06:34] Derek Patel: LlamaIndex is fine but watch chunk sizes and overlap; tokenization differences can impact prompt length accounting. We provide helper utilities for token counts in the SDK. Also note model differences — embeddings vs text-gen call shapes.
[06:50] Priya Rao: This is very helpful. Quick clarification on rate-limits: is the burst window per minute or per second?
[06:58] Maya Chen: We support both per-second and per-minute configs. For Dedicated we can tune burst windows larger; for hosted there's a default 60rps per-tenant soft limit with token-based throttles layered on.
[07:12] Liam O'Connor: Great. Would love to see the LangChain example integrated with our retrieval pipeline.
[07:17] Derek Patel: We'll share a LangChain notebook wired to a sample vector store and our SDK; it includes retrieval-augmented generation patterns and observability hooks.
[07:25] Maya Chen: Ok closing time — recap and next steps.
[07:27] Maya Chen: Action items: we'll send POC proposal and pricing, security pack, and LangChain/LlamaIndex examples. You (Nebula) will confirm POC scope and provide an initial list of prompts/testset.
[07:40] Priya Rao: Sounds good. We'll aim to get you a testset and confirm stake holders by end of week.
[07:46] Maya Chen: Perfect. Thanks all.
[07:48] Liam O'Connor: Thanks, bye.
[07:49] (call ends)
